summary:
Lesotho does not criminalise same-sex conduct. The common-law offence of sodomy was struck down in 2012, and male same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since; sexual activity between women was never criminalised. No general anti-discrimination protections exist for LGBTIQ+ people. A joint stakeholder submission to the Universal Periodic Review filed in October 2024 by The Advocates for Human Rights, the Master of Healing Foundation and the Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho confirms that same-sex conduct is lawful while recording the absence of protections. The International Commission of Jurists, in a November 2024 UPR submission, listed LGBTIQ+ rights to equality and non-discrimination among its three principal concerns for the country.

There is no legal gender recognition. No statute provides a route to change the gender marker on official documents. A 2017 constitutional analysis by the Southern African Litigation Centre argues that section 4(1) of the constitution, which refers to 'sex' and 'other status', should be read to include gender identity, consistent with the position of the UN Human Rights Committee, but no law gives effect to that reading. A briefing published in October 2020 by the Southern African Litigation Centre, the People's Matrix Association and the Women and Law in Southern Africa Research and Education Project, researched by Prof Alex Müller with community consultations, sets out the absence of any statutory route against international best practice.

The 2017 analysis warns that a transgender person travelling on a passport whose gender marker does not match their presentation could be charged with an offence. The National Identity Cards Act 9 of 2011, section 8(1), requires the Director to take reasonably practicable steps to keep personal information in the Register complete, accurate and updated; this has been read as possibly permitting a change of legal gender on identity documents, but no procedure, eligibility criteria, penalties or records of granted changes are documented.

Marriage is restricted to opposite-sex couples under the Marriage Act No. 10 of 1974 and customary law. Same-sex marriages and civil unions are not recognised. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to have that relationship recognised.

The October 2024 UPR submission documents discrimination, rape and assaults against LGBT people, barriers to health and education services, and community-level discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and expression. Reports describe discrimination in employment, health care, housing and education, with many LGBTI Basotho living secret lives and concealing their sexual orientation. Family rejection, violence and harassment are described as not uncommon.

The Matrix Support Group, established in 2009 and registered in 2010, is the only known LGBTI organisation in the country. It has operated freely across all ten districts and maintains a working relationship with the Lesotho Mounted Police Service. In December 2015 police intervened to enable a lesbian who had been forced from her home by her brothers to return, and police provided an escort for a march of approximately 200 people from Lakeside to Central Park in Maseru on 21 May. The first pride march was held on 18 May 2013 in central Maseru with a supportive police escort, and marches have been held annually since, attracting a few hundred people.

No transgender-specific provisions govern screening, sex-segregated facilities, custody, detention or gender-affirming care. The 2016 United States Department of State human rights report recorded societal discrimination and official insensitivity toward LGBTI persons, described same-sex relationships as taboo and not openly discussed, and noted that no assaults were reported while incidents often went unreported for fear of stigma. No source documents societal tolerance of transgender people specifically; the only tolerance assessment available is general to the LGBTIQ+ community, describing attitudes as slowly becoming more tolerant.
tangentialFactors:
Historical accounts document boukonchana or inkotshane, boy-wives who typically dressed as women; by 1941 public cross-dressing was commonplace. A 1914 colonial attempt to suppress the practice failed, and recent discussion of it has faced suppression and widespread denial.

Lesotho has the second highest HIV prevalence in the world, with reportedly 25 percent of Basotho infected. LGBTIQ+ activists reach out to HIV-positive people with prevention strategies.

The 2016 State Department report stated that the law at that time prohibited consensual sexual relations between men but that authorities did not enforce it, which conflicts with the 2012 date for the striking down of the sodomy offence. Deputy Prime Minister Mothetjoa Metsing said in June, after the UN General Assembly High-Level Meeting on HIV/AIDS, that the government would look into decriminalising same-sex relationships to curb HIV transmission.
localsOnly:
The Labour Act 2024 bans employment discrimination based on sexual orientation and defines workplace gender-based violence and harassment as violence and harassment, including sexual harassment, directed at workers, trainees, probationers, applicants, managers, supervisors, customers, clients, suppliers or contractors because of sex, gender or gender identity, or affecting persons of a particular sex, gender or gender identity disproportionately. The Act also covers unfair discrimination, unfair labour practice, freedom of association, and prohibitions on forced and child labour. The 2017 analysis noted that the earlier Labour Code's non-discrimination clause omitted gender and sexual orientation.

Section 127(4) of the Children's Protection and Welfare Act 2011 prohibits unfair discrimination based on sexual orientation in the selection of a diversion programme, process or option, with equal access for all children.

Since 2013 the Credit Reporting Regulations provide that credit information relating to sexual orientation may not be contained in credit bureau records except to the extent it is self-evident from marital status and family member list.

Under the Child Welfare and Protection Act 2011 only married opposite-sex couples may adopt jointly; single men and same-sex couples are not permitted to adopt.

The Matrix Support Group, established in 2009, works for an environment in which LGBTI individuals can freely express their human rights and contribute socially, politically and economically regardless of gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation and sex, principally through engagement with partner organisations on gender-based violence.
outOfScopeNotes:
The National Identity Cards Act 9 of 2011 provision on updating the Register has not been tested in any sourced procedure; eligibility criteria, penalties and any granted changes are not documented.

No source documents societal tolerance of transgender people specifically.

The 2016 State Department statement that consensual relations between men were prohibited but unenforced conflicts with the 2012 legalisation date; the discrepancy is unresolved in the sources.

No transgender-specific provisions on screening, sex-segregated facilities, custody, detention or gender-affirming care are sourced; the absence of material is not evidence either way.
